title: Top 10 Overused Verbs and Their Precise Synonyms for the Intermediate Plateau
dek: Ten “safe” verbs do too much of your talking. Learn what each one really means in a sentence, which exact verb to use instead, and which traps to avoid, with maps, quizzes and a 7-day plan.

blocks.text:
⛰️ Vol. 2026.09 — Me vs Intermediate Plateau

Special Edition: Breaking the B1–B2 Ceiling

Welcome to our September notebook special issue! Discover natural upgrades, stronger adjectives, and precise verb synonyms to overcome the intermediate plateau.

Say these five sentences out loud: **I got an email. I got the job. I got tired. I got to the station. I got a new phone.** One tiny word, five completely different meanings. A native speaker understands all five at once, but a learner who *only* has *got* sounds vague. Not wrong, just flat.

blocks.text: That flatness is the heart of the **intermediate plateau** (roughly B1–B2). Your grammar is fine and people understand you, but ten very common verbs are doing most of the work: **get, make, do, have, go, say, think, look, know, give**. They are not bad words, and you will keep using them every day. The trick is to notice when a more exact verb is waiting right behind them.

blocks.text: The 3-step upgrade 1. Notice — Catch a safe verb as you speak or write. “I got a new phone.” 2. Ask — What exactly happened? Pick the real meaning. Did I buy it? Win it? Was it a gift? 3. Choose — Use the verb that matches, then check it fits the situation. “I bought a new phone.”

blocks.text: I want to say get… what do I really mean? Which meaning is it? Something arrived for you → receive. You paid for it → buy. You work for the money → earn. You arrived somewhere → reach / arrive at. You boarded a bus or train → catch / take. You understood → understand / follow. Something changed → improve / rise / grow.

blocks.text: 1. get
blocks.say: 1. get. The champion of vagueness: one verb, at least eight meanings.

items: **receive** (you receive something) — I got your message yesterday. → I received your message yesterday. Receive is a little more formal than get, perfect for emails and work.
**buy** (you buy something) — I got a new phone. → I bought a new phone.
**earn** (you earn money) — She gets €2,000 a month. → She earns €2,000 a month.
**obtain / secure** (you obtain something official) — He got a visa. → He obtained a visa. Add the idea of effort with secure: She secured a place at university.
**improve / rise / grow** (something changes) — Things got better. → Things improved. Numbers go up? Use rise or grow: Prices rose last year.
**arrive at / reach** (you arrive somewhere) — We got to the hotel at six. → We arrived at the hotel at six. Arrive at a place, in a city. Reach needs no preposition: We reached the hotel at six.
**understand / follow** (you understand) — I don’t get it. → Sorry, I’m not following. I don’t get it is fine with friends. In a meeting, I’m not following sounds more polite.
**catch / take** (you board a bus or train) — I got the 8:15 train. → I caught the 8:15 train. Catch = you must be on time. Take = your normal way to travel: I take the bus to work.
⚠️ Trap: Get is not wrong: I got tired is natural speech. Upgrade when a more exact verb exists and when you write. ✗ I arrived to the station. → ✓ I arrived at the station.

blocks.text: 2. make
blocks.say: 2. make. Make means create or cause. Very often, a more exact verb is hiding inside the phrase.

items: **create / develop / design** (you create something new) — They made a new app. → They created a new app. Develop = built step by step. Design = planned how it looks and works.
**produce / manufacture** (a company produces goods) — The factory makes bikes. → The factory produces bikes.
**cook / prepare / build** (you cook or build) — I made dinner for everyone. → I cooked dinner for everyone. Build = made from parts: He built a bookshelf.
**simplify / clarify / shorten** (make + adjective = one verb) — This app makes my life easier. → This app simplifies my life. She made the rules clear → She clarified the rules.

**decide / suggest / compare / complain** (make + noun = hidden verb) — We made a decision to move. → We decided to move. make a suggestion → suggest · make a comparison → compare · make a complaint → complain
⚠️ Trap: These collocations stay with make: make a mistake, make progress, make an effort, make money. ✗ I did a mistake. → ✓ I made a mistake.

blocks.text: 3. do
blocks.say: 3. do. Do is a blank cheque: it takes its meaning from the noun. Say the real action instead.

items: **complete / finish** (you finish a task) — I did the report on Friday. → I completed the report on Friday. Finish is the everyday word; complete sounds more official.
**carry out / conduct** (you carry out formal work) — We did a survey. → We carried out a survey. Carry out suits plans, tests and studies. Conduct suits surveys, interviews and experiments.
**take care of / handle** (you deal with a problem) — Don’t worry, I’ll do it. → Don’t worry, I’ll take care of it. She handled the complaint calmly.
**play / go / do** (you do sport) — I do tennis on Saturdays. → I play tennis on Saturdays. play + ball games · go + -ing (go running, go swimming) · do + individual practice (do yoga, do judo)
**take / give / hold** (exams, talks, meetings) — I did a presentation. → I gave a presentation. take an exam · give a presentation · hold a meeting (or have a meeting)
⚠️ Trap: ✗ do a photo → ✓ take a photo · ✗ do a party → ✓ have / throw a party · ✗ do a decision → ✓ make a decision

blocks.text: 4. have
blocks.say: 4. have. Have can mean own, contain, experience… or almost nothing at all.

items: **own / possess** (you own something) — My uncle has a small farm. → My uncle owns a small farm.
**contain / include** (something contains parts) — The report has three sections. → The report contains three sections. Include = part of a bigger list: The price includes breakfast.

**go through / experience / face** (you live through an experience) — We had a difficult year. → We went through a difficult year. Face a problem · experience delays · enjoy yourself: We enjoyed the trip.
**argue / rest / try** (have + noun = hidden verb) — We had an argument about money. → We argued about money. have a rest → rest · have a try → try · have a look → look
**eat / drink** (you eat or drink) — I had a sandwich. → I ate a sandwich. Have lunch and have a coffee are natural, so keep them. Use eat and drink when you want to be exact.
⚠️ Trap: In English you are your age and your feelings: ✗ I have 25 years. → ✓ I’m 25. · ✗ I have hunger. → ✓ I’m hungry.

blocks.text: 5. go
blocks.say: 5. go. Go only says “move away”. Say how you travel, why, or where to.

items: **walk / stroll / hike** (on foot) — We went to the beach. → We walked to the beach. Stroll = slow and relaxed. Hike = a long walk in nature.
**drive / fly / cycle / take** (by transport) — We went to Spain last summer. → We flew to Spain last summer. We took the train to Madrid.
**attend / visit** (you attend an event) — I went to the conference. → I attended the conference. Visit people and places: I visited my grandparents.
**leave / set off / depart** (you leave) — The bus goes at seven. → The bus leaves at seven. Set off = start a journey: We set off at dawn.
**head / make your way** (you move towards) — She went to the exit. → She headed for the exit. Make your way to = go, often through a crowd or a difficult place.
**turn out / work out** (things develop) — It went well in the end. → It turned out well in the end. Turn out = the final result. Work out = problems get solved: Don’t worry, it’ll work out.
⚠️ Trap: ✗ I’ll go to home. → ✓ I’ll go home. (no to before home) · ✗ I arrived to Paris. → ✓ I arrived in Paris.

blocks.text: 6. say
blocks.say: 6. say. Say just reports words. Pick a verb that shows why and how they were said.

items: **inform / tell / mention** (you give information) — He said that the meeting was cancelled. → He informed us that the meeting was cancelled. Tell needs a person: He told me. Mention = say briefly: She mentioned a problem.
**explain / describe** (you make it clear) — She said how the machine works. → She explained how the machine works.
**announce / state** (you make it official) — The company said it will close two shops. → The company announced that it will close two shops.
**claim** (you say it, but without proof) — He says he never saw the email. → He claims he never saw the email. Claim signals “maybe true, maybe not”.

**argue / point out / suggest** (you give reasons for a view) — She said we need more time. → She argued that we need more time. Point out = draw attention to a fact: He pointed out a mistake. Suggest = propose an idea.
**admit / deny** (you say it is true / not true) — He said he broke the window. → He admitted breaking the window. Deny = say it is not true: She denied taking the money.
**whisper / shout / mutter** (how it sounds) — She said quietly, “Be careful.” → She whispered, “Be careful.” Mutter = say quietly and unclearly, often when you are annoyed.
⚠️ Trap: Tell needs a person, say does not: ✗ He said me the truth. → ✓ He told me the truth. · ✗ He told that he was late. → ✓ He said (that) he was late.

blocks.text: 7. think
blocks.say: 7. think. Think hides how sure you are. Choose a verb that shows your level of certainty.

items: **believe / feel** (you have an opinion) — I think this is a good idea. → I believe this is a good idea. I feel that… sounds softer and more personal.
**suppose / guess / imagine** (you are guessing) — I think he’s at home. → I suppose he’s at home.
**assume** (you accept it without checking) — I thought you knew. → I assumed you knew.
**suspect** (you have a bad feeling) — I think he lied. → I suspect he lied. Suspect usually means you believe something is wrong or dishonest.
**consider / weigh up / reflect on** (you are weighing options) — I’m thinking about the offer. → I’m considering the offer.
**wonder** (you don’t have the answer) — I’m thinking about what will happen next. → I wonder what will happen next.
**conclude / realise** (you reach a conclusion) — We thought we needed more time. → We concluded that we needed more time. Realise = you suddenly understand: I realised I had no keys.

blocks.text: 8. look
blocks.say: 8. look. Look only says “use your eyes”. English has a different verb for every kind of looking.

items: **glance at** (a very quick look) — She looked at her watch quickly. → She glanced at her watch.

**watch / observe** (you follow something that moves) — The scientists looked at the birds for a week. → The scientists observed the birds for a week. look at = something still (a photo) · watch = something that moves or happens (a film, a match) · see = it just enters your eyes.
**stare at / gaze at** (a long, fixed look) — He looked at me for ages. → He stared at me. Stare can feel rude. Gaze is calm and dreamy: She gazed at the sea.

**examine / inspect / check** (a careful look to find out) — The doctor looked at my knee. → The doctor examined my knee. Inspect is official: An officer inspected the building. Check is the everyday word.
**seem / appear** (it seems to be) — The results look good. → The results seem promising. The results appear to be correct is more formal.
**search for / look up** (you try to find something) — I’m looking for my keys. → I’m searching for my keys. Look after a child or a pet = take care of it.
⚠️ Trap: Look needs at, and TV is for watching: ✗ Look the photo. → ✓ Look at the photo. · ✗ I look TV. → ✓ I watch TV.

blocks.text: 9. know
blocks.say: 9. know. Know is a state, so it hides what happened or what you can do.

items: **understand / see** (you understand it) — I know the problem. → I understand the problem.
**realise** (you suddenly see the truth) — Now I know I was wrong. → Now I realise I was wrong.
**recognise** (you have seen it before) — I know that face. → I recognise that face.
**be familiar with / be aware of** (you have heard of it) — Do you know this app? → Are you familiar with this app? Be aware of = you have noticed it exists: Are you aware of the risks?
**speak / can / be good at** (you have a skill) — I know French. → I speak French. I can cook / I’m good at cooking, not I know to cook.
**find out / learn / discover** (the moment you learn it) — I knew the news yesterday. → I found out the news yesterday. Know is a state. Use find out for the moment it happened.
⚠️ Trap: State verbs with since or for need the present perfect: ✗ I know him since 2019. → ✓ I’ve known him since 2019.

blocks.text: 10. give
blocks.say: 10. give. Give is correct, but a more exact verb says what kind of giving it was.

items: **provide / offer / supply** (you provide help or a service) — We give free Wi-Fi. → We provide free Wi-Fi. Offer = say you are ready to give: She offered to help.
**hand / pass / deliver** (you pass something to a person) — She gave me the keys. → She handed me the keys. Deliver = take to a place: The courier delivered the parcel.
**grant / award / allow** (an authority allows or rewards) — They gave me permission to leave early. → They granted me permission to leave early. Award = a prize or a grade: She was awarded a medal.
**donate / lend** (you give money or things) — He gave a lot of money to the school. → He donated a lot of money to the school. Lend = you want it back: Can you lend me your pen?
**advise / recommend** (you give advice) — My teacher gave me some advice. → My teacher advised me to read more.
⚠️ Trap: Advice has no plural: ✗ He gave me an advice. → ✓ He gave me some advice. (or He advised me).

blocks.question: She ___ at her phone quickly and put it away.

blocks.text: *Get* and *make* are not your enemies. Native speakers use them all day. The goal is **choice**: knowing that a more exact verb exists, and having it ready when it helps you sound clearer, kinder or more convincing. Pick **one** verb this week, master its card, then move on to the next. That is how B1 becomes B2.

blocks.title: Learning French, Italian, Russian or Greek?
blocks.content: The plateau looks the same in every language, but each language has its own “safe” verbs (*faire, fare, делать, κάνω*…). Use **Read in** at the top of the page: each version is written for that language, not translated word for word.
